# WHERE THEY COME, AND WHAT STAYS

## A sustainable tourism development plan for the Region
### Demand creation, absorptive capacity, and uninvited demand as three separate decisions

**Regional Assembly decision paper | v2.0**
*Prepared by the Regional Tourism Agency (RTA) for the Assembly, the Municipal Leaders' Board, and the four statutory partners named in §2.1. Drafted on the assumption of full publication under access-to-information law; there is no confidential annex to the argument, only to the vendor pricing in Annex 4.*

*Annexes (not required for this decision): A1 site-by-site capacity models; A2 municipal consent schedules; A3 research brief and survey instruments; A4 procurement pricing; A5 the scoring model as a live spreadsheet.*

---

## Decision sought — split into what is reversible and what is not

The Assembly is asked to take **six reversible decisions today** and to take **no irreversible decision at all**. This split is deliberate: public bodies are routinely asked to approve a bundle, and the bundle is then treated as a mandate for the irreversible parts. This paper refuses that.

**Part A — approvals sought today (all reversible within one budget year, all revocable by simple Assembly majority)**

| # | Approval | Reversible because |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | The **three-track structure** (Demand / Capacity / Uninvited Demand) as the organising form of the programme | It is an internal work-breakdown; abandoning it costs re-drafting |
| A2 | The **selection method** for source segments (§3.2) and first cluster (§10.1), including publication of the full scoring model and its weights | Method can be re-weighted; publication is one-way but harmless |
| A3 | The **positioning boundary and claims regime** in §4 — i.e. what the Region will *not* say about itself | A negative constraint; lifting it costs nothing but credibility |
| A4 | The **capacity rule** in §6.2 (Limits of Acceptable Change; posted cap derived from the first binding constraint) and the response ladder in §6.5 | Thresholds are provisional until Gate 1 and revisable annually |
| A5 | The **replacement of "international arrivals" as the agency's headline KPI** with the four-metric set in §12.1, effective next reporting cycle | Reporting change; arrivals continue to be published as a diagnostic |
| A6 | **€[2.1]m, plus €[0.31]m contingency, to fund Gate 0** (build in §11.1). Note that €[1.24]m of this is work the Region owes under statutory obligations regardless of this programme (§11.2) | Studies have standalone value; ~59% is non-discretionary spend brought forward |

**Part B — decisions explicitly *not* sought today, reserved to Gate 1 after Assembly debate on the Gate 0 evidence**

Cluster designation; any route development support; any paid brand campaign in any market; any visitor levy; any short-let regulation; any capital works; any interagency compact signature that binds a partner's capital programme; any target for visitor numbers.

**And one thing the Assembly is asked to accept in advance:** that Gate 0 may return a result that stops this programme (§3.6, §13.3). The plan is designed so that stopping is a normal, non-embarrassing outcome that has already been paid for.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

"Developing tourism" is not one decision. **Demand creation**, **absorptive capacity**, and the management of **demand nobody invited** run on different clocks, are owned by different institutions, and fail in different ways; fusing them into a single master plan is how regions with genuine assets arrive at degraded assets, resentful residents, and a margin that leaves the Region on the same aircraft the visitor did. The clock asymmetry is not the simple one usually cited. *Cheap, price-led, short-stay demand* can be created in roughly [12]–[24] months and can also arrive with no help from us at all — driven by carrier route economics, cruise berthing, short-let platform supply, currency, and social virality, none of which the RTA controls **[R]**. The *long-stay, off-peak, provenance-paying* demand this plan wants takes closer to [36]–[60] months to build **[R]**. Wastewater headroom, a maintained trail network, trained guides, conservation of built fabric, and durable resident consent take [4]–[8] years and, critically, are **not in the RTA's gift** (§2.1). So the Region faces two independent sequencing risks: our own marketing outrunning our capacity, and *other people's* demand outrunning it regardless. This plan therefore proposes a **Demand Track** built segment-first — off-peak, longer-stay, low-travel-emission catchments selected on the published criteria in §3.2, with long-haul markets **opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); a **Capacity Track** governed not by a single carrying-capacity number but by a **Limits of Acceptable Change** framework in which the posted operational cap is derived from whichever constraint binds first — in our candidate clusters, on current evidence, summer wastewater loading and trailhead parking (§6.2); and a **Demand Management Track** with a legal-instrument inventory for demand we did not create (§7). The three tracks are bound together by one enforcement mechanism, and it is the most important sentence in this paper: **Demand Track expenditure is escrowed and released only against certified Capacity Track milestones (§2.4).** Marketing money that cannot be spent until the treatment plant is consented is the only structural defence against a sequencing error, because exhortation is not one. Positioning is *not* "undiscovered," "hidden gem," or "the next [comparator]"; those framings sell scarcity, and scarcity sold is scarcity ended (§4.1). We propose a **still-in-use region** positioning — a working landscape and a living culture that receives guests, offering access to practice rather than performance — with the access itself governed by a community consent architecture that includes an unconditional right of withdrawal (§9). Community benefit is engineered into instruments — licensing, procurement rules, a ring-fenced levy, housing controls, a wage floor, a career pathway — because as an adjective it does not survive contact with a balance sheet (§8). Three claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not asserted**: that the target segment exists at the volume our Year-5 economics assume; that the first cluster's water, wastewater and access can carry that load without capital the Region cannot raise; and that there is **standing social licence for international tourism growth at all**. Gate 0 tests exactly these three, and §3.6 and §13.3 state in advance what results would change or end the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to residents

### 0.1 How to read the figures — four kinds of number

Confusing these is the main way tourism master plans mislead their own authors, and the main way they mislead assemblies.

| Tag | Type | Examples in this paper | How certain | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** — law, licence, consent, statutory limit | Wastewater discharge consent (Population Equivalent, peak factor); water abstraction licence volumes; Natura 2000 site boundaries and Habitats Directive Art. 6(3) triggers; SEA/EIA screening thresholds; Water Framework Directive status objectives; heritage designation and World Heritage buffer-zone rules; short-let registration duties under the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation; state aid rules on airport/airline start-up aid; procurement thresholds; the Region's legal power to levy a visitor charge; UCPD / Empowering Consumers Directive constraints on green claims | Should be **certain** — verify, never estimate. A [V] item estimated is a legal risk carried unpriced | Gate 0: counsel, licensed engineers, the competent environmental authority. See full list §0.5 |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Current arrivals and bed-nights; seasonality index; visitor spend and leakage; competitor pricing; segment size; carbon per visitor-night; resident sentiment | Official statistics ±[10]%; commercial trade data ±[15]%; **niche segment sizing ±[40]% at best**; stated-preference willingness-to-pay ±[50]% and systematically optimistic | Gate 0: field research, conjoint, trade interviews, representative survey |
| **[D]** | **Design target** — a choice, not a discovery | Year-5 retained value per visitor-night; cluster count; levy rate; length-of-stay floor for long-haul promotion; channel mix | Not uncertain — *undecided*. Presenting a design target as a forecast is the commonest failure in these documents | Gate 1: this Assembly, by vote |
| **[C]** | **Contested** — legitimately disputed value judgement or politically determined variable | How much crowding residents will accept; whether heritage access is a right or a resource; the equity claim of non-cluster municipalities; whether a levy is a tax; the acceptable trade between jobs now and fabric later | **Cannot be resolved by evidence.** Evidence can only narrow the question | Assembly deliberation, statutory consultation, and the deliberative panel in §2.5. Never by the RTA alone |

The **[C]** tag exists because a public plan that disguises value choices as technical findings will be found out, and should be. Every [C] item in this paper is flagged, and none of them is decided by this paper.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out of scope (and why) |
|---|---|
| One international demand programme, built segment-first, entering through one receiving cluster | Domestic and same-country visitor marketing — a separate, larger, already-funded programme; but domestic visitors **are** counted in all capacity calculations (§6) |
| One first receiving cluster of [3]–[4] municipalities, plus the published queue and capacity fund for the rest (§10) | Designating clusters two and three — Gate 2, no earlier than Year [3] |
| Absorptive capacity assessment and the interagency compact required to build it (§2) | Delivering the capacity works themselves — those belong to the utility, the roads authority and the heritage ministry and require their own approvals |
| Instruments for local value retention, housing, labour and cultural consent (§8, §9) | General regional economic development, agricultural policy, or housing supply policy beyond tourism-attributable effects |
| Management of demand the Region did not create (§7) | Aviation policy, cruise line commercial strategy, platform regulation at national level — we can only use the levers we hold (§7.3) |
| Statutory environmental assessment of this plan (SEA), initiated at Gate 0 | Project-level EIA/Appropriate Assessment for individual works — sequenced after Gate 1 |

# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.

We propose a **still-in-use region** positioning — a working landscape and a living culture that receives guests, offering access to practice rather than performance — with the access itself governed by a community consent architecture that includes an unconditional right of withdrawal (§9). Community benefit is engineered into instruments — licensing, procurement rules, a ring-fenced levy, housing controls, a wage floor, a career pathway — because as an adjective it does not survive contact with a balance sheet (§8). Three claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not asserted**: that the target segment exists at the volume our Year-5 economics assume; that the first cluster's water, wastewater and access can carry that load without capital the Region cannot raise; and that there is **standing social licence for international tourism growth at all**. Gate 0 tests exactly these three, and §3.6 and §13.3 state in advance what results would change or end the recommendation.

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to residents

### 0.1 How to read the figures — four kinds of number

Confusing these is the main way tourism master plans mislead their own authors, and the main way they mislead assemblies.

| Tag | Type | Examples in this paper | How certain | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** — law, licence, consent, statutory limit | Wastewater discharge consent (Population Equivalent, peak factor); water abstraction licence volumes; Natura 2000 site boundaries and Habitats Directive Art. 6(3) triggers; SEA/EIA screening thresholds; Water Framework Directive status objectives; heritage designation and World Heritage buffer-zone rules; short-let registration duties under the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation; state aid rules on airport/airline start-up aid; procurement thresholds; the Region's legal power to levy a visitor charge; UCPD / Empowering Consumers Directive constraints on green claims | Should be **certain** — verify, never estimate. A [V] item estimated is a legal risk carried unpriced | Gate 0: counsel, licensed engineers, the competent environmental authority. See full list §0.5 |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Current arrivals and bed-nights; seasonality index; visitor spend and leakage; competitor pricing; segment size; carbon per visitor-night; resident sentiment | Official statistics ±[10]%; commercial trade data ±[15]%; **niche segment sizing ±[40]% at best**; stated-preference willingness-to-pay ±[50]% and systematically optimistic | Gate 0: field research, conjoint, trade interviews, representative survey |
| **[D]** | **Design target** — a choice, not a discovery | Year-5 retained value per visitor-night; cluster count; levy rate; length-of-stay floor for long-haul promotion; channel mix | Not uncertain — *undecided*. Presenting a design target as a forecast is the commonest failure in these documents | Gate 1: this Assembly, by vote |
| **[C]** | **Contested** — legitimately disputed value judgement or politically determined variable | How much crowding residents will accept; whether heritage access is a right or a resource; the equity claim of non-cluster municipalities; whether a levy is a tax; the acceptable trade between jobs now and fabric later | **Cannot be resolved by evidence.** Evidence can only narrow the question | Assembly deliberation, statutory consultation, and the deliberative panel in §2.5. Never by the RTA alone |

The **[C]** tag exists because a public plan that disguises value choices as technical findings will be found out, and should be. Every [C] item in this paper is flagged, and none of them is decided by this paper.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out of scope (and why) |
|---|---|
| One international demand programme, built segment-first, entering through one receiving cluster | Domestic and same-country visitor marketing — a separate, larger, already-funded programme; but domestic visitors **are** counted in all capacity calculations (§6) |
| One first receiving cluster of [3]–[4] municipalities, plus the published queue and capacity fund for the rest (§10) | Designating clusters two and three — Gate 2, no earlier than Year [3] |
| Absorptive capacity assessment and the interagency compact required to build it (§2) | Delivering the capacity works themselves — those belong to the utility, the roads authority and the heritage ministry and require their own approvals |
| Instruments for local value retention, housing, labour and cultural consent (§8, §9) | General regional economic development, agricultural policy, or housing supply policy beyond tourism-attributable effects |
| Management of demand the Region did not create (§7) | Aviation policy, cruise line commercial strategy, platform regulation at national level — we can only use the levers we hold (§7.3) |
